e.t: Abar, also rendered Avar, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:17. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identifying rather than conceptual: it points to a particular named individual in the genealogical record. The word should therefore be read as a personal designation, with the surrounding verse supplying the person’s place in that record.

Abichail, also represented as Avikhel, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal name used in genealogical and tribal records. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific individuals bearing this name cannot be distinguished here; the lexical meaning remains the name itself rather than a broader concept.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something that is unclear or unseen—something not plainly understood or not visible. It can point either to a lack of clarity or to something hidden from sight, depending on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Psalms, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Akkarioth is a proper name, referring to a specific named place or entity rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears only once, at Jeremiah 31:41. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Akkariōth” or “Akkarioth,” but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so its precise role in that passage cannot be described further.

This word means “read”: to take in written words and understand or recite them. It is a verb describing the act of reading, especially when written material is being presented or consulted. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 53 times, showing regular use for reading written words rather than naming a person, object, or abstract idea. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being read and how the surrounding sentence uses the action.

Anaia, also rendered Anea, is a proper name identifying a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the LXX, at Nehemiah 10:23. The available information establishes the name’s form and location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, family, or place. Its meaning is therefore best represented as the proper name itself rather than expanded into an inferred description.

This Greek LXX verb means “renew”: to make something new again or restore it to renewed condition. It describes an act of renewal rather than a person or object itself. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Esther, Job, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being renewed and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means a bearer or a carrying pole. It can refer either to someone who carries something or to a pole used for carrying an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 18 times across 16 verses, especially in Exodus, Numbers, and Chronicles. Its precise sense depends on whether the surrounding sentence is naming a person who carries or a physical implement used to transport something.

Aniam is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:19. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identification, but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or explanation of the person beyond the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding genealogical context.

This word is a proper name for a person called “Antiocheus” or “Antiokhefs.” It does not describe a general quality or action; it identifies an individual by name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees 4, at 4:9 and 4:19. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s role in either passage.

This verb means to treasure something or store it away for safekeeping. It describes deliberately placing something valuable in reserve rather than using or discarding it immediately. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 3:4. The word’s central idea is preserving something precious so that it remains available and secure. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of treasuring or storing away.

This verb means to turn someone or something away, or to alienate them. It describes a movement away from a person, place, purpose, or relationship, and can also express causing that separation. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, occurring 431 times across 413 verses. Its basic sense remains consistent, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is physical turning, rejection, or relational estrangement.

This noun means a “terse pointed saying; apophthegm”—a brief statement expressed in a memorable, striking way. It refers to a compact saying rather than a long speech or extended explanation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and Ezekiel, so it is uncommon within this corpus. The surrounding verse determines what the particular saying communicates, but the word itself emphasizes the saying’s concise and pointed character.

Asiedōth, also rendered Asiethoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular place or location in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek form of the Old Testament, at Joshua 15:47. Without the surrounding verse text, its location within the list of places cannot be explained further, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a geographic name.

This noun means a “path with no turnings”: a route that proceeds directly rather than bending or winding. It identifies a straightforward way or track, with the central idea being the absence of turns. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times across Judges, Job, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a direct, unturning path.

This noun means “menstruation,” referring to a woman’s monthly bodily bleeding. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used in passages that discuss the condition itself and the ritual-cleanliness regulations associated with it. The word occurs 11 times across 8 verses, mostly in Leviticus, with one occurrence in Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the menstrual period or the bleeding connected with it.

Achōi; Akhi is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:29. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name itself can be stated confidently, while the person’s particular role must be understood from that passage’s context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Badaia” and also associated with the form “Vathea.” It identifies a named individual or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:35. The supplied lexical information gives the name’s form and rendering, but the verse text is not included here, so its specific role in that passage cannot be described further.

Balei, also rendered Vali, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, with each occurrence in a different verse. The name is found in Numbers 26:42, Jeremiah 17:8, Hosea 14:6, and Habakkuk 1:10. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific person or referent cannot be identified here, but its basic function is to designate a named individual or entity in those passages.

This adjective means “foreigner,” describing someone regarded as coming from another people or place. It identifies a person as an outsider in relation to the community or group being discussed, rather than naming a particular person or nation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs seven times. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a person viewed as foreign to those speaking or acting.

This word means “grinding,” referring to the action or process of grinding. It is a noun, so it names the activity rather than describing someone as grinding. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in Sirach. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains the act of grinding. The word’s stated meaning does not by itself identify what is being ground or explain the purpose of the action.

This Greek LXX noun means a “dyke” or “dam”—a structure built to hold back, block, or control water. It refers to a physical barrier rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings preserved in this corpus: once in Isaiah 37:25 and once in 2 Maccabees 12:13. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “dark,” describing the absence or reduction of light. It can identify something characterized by darkness, whether referring to physical surroundings or another context where the surrounding passage supplies the precise force. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 10:21. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it describes what is dark. The reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text to explain any further nuance in that verse.

This noun means “ball” or “small globe,” referring to a rounded object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles 4:12–13. The basic meaning points to a compact, spherical form rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding description, but the word itself identifies a rounded object.

This Greek LXX verb means to discriminate—distinguishing or judging between things—and can also mean to doubt. It describes an act of discernment or hesitation rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word appears 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Job, Ezekiel, and other books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding context emphasizes making a judgment or wavering in uncertainty.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprinkle with”: to scatter or apply a substance in small drops over something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 7:17, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains the act of sprinkling something onto or over another thing.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Half
e.t: This noun means “half”: one of two parts into which something is divided. It can refer to a portion produced by cutting or separating an object, rather than to the whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Ezekiel. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on what has been divided and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “bribe”: to give or use a bribe in order to influence someone improperly. It describes bribery as an action rather than naming the payment itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The word’s central idea remains the use of gifts or payments to gain an unfair decision, favor, or advantage. The surrounding passage determines who is bribing and what outcome is being sought.

This noun means “dissimulation”: the act of hiding one’s true intention or feeling behind a false appearance. It describes deliberate pretense rather than open and sincere conduct. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is concealed purpose expressed through deceptive behavior.

This verb describes someone being awestruck—deeply affected by what they see, hear, or experience. It presents a person as overwhelmed with wonder or amazement rather than simply noticing something. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Ecclesiastes, Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “expire,” describing the ending of a person’s life. As a verb, it expresses what someone does or comes to do rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in Ezekiel 21:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the coming to an end of life.

This adjective describes someone “born in the house,” meaning the person was born within the household rather than being identified by a separate place of origin. It functions as a descriptive word for a person’s birth status. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 18:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: a person born in the household.

This verb means to “usurp authority”: to take or exercise authority that does not properly belong to the person doing so. It describes an action rather than a person or title. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach. The surrounding verse wording is needed to show exactly who is acting and how the misuse of authority functions in each passage, but the word’s central sense remains an improper taking or exercising of authority.

This Greek LXX verb means “fasten from.” It describes an act of fastening in relation to a particular point or source. Because it is a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This Greek LXX verb means to set something up again or restore it. It describes the act of putting something back into a proper or previous condition, rather than merely beginning something new. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains renewal through reestablishing what had been damaged, displaced, or brought low.

This Greek LXX verb means “roll down upon.” It describes an action in which something is rolled downward onto or against something else. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Joshua 10:27. As a verb, it expresses movement or an act rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being rolled down.

This adverb means “seven-fold,” describing something done or present in an amount multiplied by seven. It expresses a seven-times measure rather than naming an object, person, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: four times in Old Testament passages and once in Sirach. Its exact force—whether describing quantity, intensity, or repetition—depends on the sentence where it appears, but its central idea remains a sevenfold measure.

This adjective describes something as “bruised pounded.” It points to material that has been struck, crushed, or beaten so that its condition is marked by that treatment. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears once, in Leviticus 2:14. Its basic meaning is therefore specific rather than broad: it identifies something prepared or affected through pounding or bruising. The surrounding verse supplies the particular object and purpose, but the word itself focuses on the object's bruised or pounded condition.

Esther is a proper name, referring to the woman known by that name in the Greek Old Testament book of Esther. It identifies the same person throughout the narrative, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs 45 times across 37 verses, all within Esther, from Esther 2:7 through Esther 10:3. Its meaning is therefore its role as a personal name: Esther. The precise significance of her actions or position belongs to the surrounding passage, not to the name itself.

This adjective describes someone or something as having a good reputation or being famous. It expresses honorable public recognition rather than merely being noticed. As an adjective, it adds this quality to a person, thing, or name being described. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah and once in Wisdom. Its basic sense remains “of good report; famous,” while the surrounding sentence determines what is receiving that description.

This verb describes someone who is willing and ready to obey. It presents obedience as an inward readiness to respond favorably to direction or authority, rather than merely describing an outward act. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is a person being inclined toward obedience.

Zai is a noun functioning as a personal name or designation, not as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs only once, at Psalm 118:49. The available lexical information identifies the word itself, but without the verse text and surrounding context, it does not establish anything further about the person or role associated with Zai. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the passage where it appears.

Eliam is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered as “Ēliam” or “Iliam.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Ezekiel 47:16. The name itself identifies the person, but the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional details about who Eliam was. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the verse and its surrounding context.

This word means “found”: to establish something securely, especially by laying its foundation. It can describe founding a structure or establishing something firmly in place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 34 times, including passages about buildings and the world’s foundations. Its basic idea is deliberate establishment, whether referring to a physical foundation or to something set securely by purposeful action.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “lament” or “dirge”—an expression of grief, especially in a mourning song or formal cry of sorrow. It names the sorrowful expression itself rather than the person who mourns. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 27:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a lament or dirge.

This verb means to treat someone medically or to cure an illness. It describes the act of providing healing care, with the result of restoring a sick or injured person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, so it expresses a focused action rather than a broad description of health or well-being. Its exact force in any passage depends on who is being treated and what condition is involved. The word appears in passages from 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah.

Ierakōn, also rendered Ierakon, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:46. The name identifies a specific entity named in that passage, while the name itself does not carry a broader ordinary meaning such as an action, quality, or relationship. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “to cheer” or “make cheerful.” It describes bringing gladness or lifting someone’s spirits, rather than merely feeling cheerful oneself. As a verb, it expresses an action directed toward producing joy or encouragement. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing once in Psalms and twice in Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is making someone or something cheerful.

This adjective describes something as “of equal value”—matching another thing in worth, strength, or significance. It presents two things as equivalent rather than ranking one above the other. In the Greek LXX material represented here, the word occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what is being compared, but its central idea remains equality in value or capacity.

This Greek LXX word is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is represented by the names “Iōsphē” and “Iosfi.” The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Genesis 47:5, so its meaning is that of a personal designation rather than a common word with a broad range of uses. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “covering”: something placed over another thing to conceal or protect it. It is used three times in the Old Testament Greek, in Exodus and Numbers, and refers to a covering associated with the tabernacle furnishings. The word identifies the covering itself rather than the act of covering. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and description of the object involved.

Kaspin is a proper name, referring to a person, place, or other named entity identified by that name. The available lexical meaning is simply “Kaspin,” so Scripture does not provide enough information here to assign it a broader descriptive meaning. In the Greek LXX corpus, Kaspin occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:13. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but as a word it functions as a name rather than as a term describing an action, quality, or relationship.

“Roll down” describes movement from a higher position to a lower one, often by turning or descending. It is a verb expressing the action of rolling downward rather than simply being below. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs three times, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broad or highly varied. Its exact force in any passage depends on what is moving and the surrounding sentence.

“Seizing” describes the act of taking something by force or possession. As a noun, this word names that action rather than serving as a command or describing a person. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 20:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains the act of seizing.

This verb means to “sigh” or “groan,” expressing an audible response to distress, burden, pain, or deep concern. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it describes the act of voicing such inner heaviness rather than merely thinking or feeling it silently. The word occurs six times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Jeremiah, Lamentations, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This noun means a scoffer—a person who treats something with contempt and expresses that attitude through mocking or disdainful speech. It identifies someone whose response is not humble acceptance but dismissive scorn. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times, in Habakkuk and Zephaniah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “capital” or “summary”: the main amount, chief part, or concise statement that gathers something into its essential point. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages involving counting people or property and presenting a condensed account. The word therefore points either to something central or to a brief summing up, depending on the sentence. Its exact sense in any particular verse comes from the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “bowls of,” referring to bowl-like vessels or containers. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 28:17. The available meaning identifies the object itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what these bowls contained or how they were used there. Thus, its ordinary sense is a plural reference to bowls or similar vessels, not an action, quality, or person.

This Greek LXX noun means “pebble,” referring to a small, rounded stone. It describes a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, once in 1 Samuel and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, but its ordinary meaning remains a small stone or pebble.

This noun means “function” or “ministry”: an assigned service or duty carried out in a recognized role. It can describe ministry as an ongoing responsibility rather than merely a single action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 47 times, with many occurrences in Numbers and Chronicles, showing its use in descriptions of organized service. The precise activity involved depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a designated function or ministry.

Maala is a proper name, referring to someone identified by that name rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Numbers 36:11 and Joshua 17:3. The name is rendered “Maala,” and no broader lexical meaning is provided. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX proper name is identified as “Madiēnaios; Mathineos.” It functions as a personal or group designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in two places in Genesis and once in Numbers. Because no verse text is provided here, its specific reference in each passage cannot be described beyond identifying it as a name used in those passages.

Masma, also rendered Mazma, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person in genealogical lists. The name occurs three times, in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, and the available renderings preserve it as “Masma.” Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its particular family connection or role in each list cannot be explained further. Its meaning is therefore its identity as the personal name Masma or Mazma.

This verb means “hiding themselves.” It describes subjects who conceal themselves from view rather than remaining openly visible. The wording presents the action as something done by the subjects themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 21:20. Its basic sense is therefore focused and specific: people withdrawing from sight or keeping themselves concealed. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation in which this action occurs.

Melchia is a personal name, referring to individuals identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is also rendered Melkhia, reflecting a spelling variant rather than a different basic meaning. The name appears nine times across nine verses, especially in Nehemiah, 1 Chronicles, and Ezra. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily the person’s identification, not a general quality, action, or object. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which Melchia is being named in a particular passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “merchant,” referring to a person who buys, sells, or trades goods. It describes people engaged in commercial exchange rather than a particular product or place. In this LXX corpus, the word occurs twice, both times in Isaiah 23, where it identifies merchants connected with the chapter’s discussion of trade. The word therefore presents a straightforward description of people involved in commerce. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a merchant or trader.

This Greek LXX verb means “reconsider” or “yield.” It describes changing one’s course or position rather than remaining fixed in a prior decision. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone rethinking what was chosen, asserted, or intended, or giving way when appropriate. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 22 times, showing regular use for a change of mind or decision. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means to “taint” or “defile”—to make something unclean or polluted. It is used 122 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, especially in Leviticus and Ezekiel, where the idea of defilement is prominent. The word can describe a person, place, or thing made unclean, but its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

“Nabataios” or “Navateos” is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek LXX text. It is not presented here as a common description or action word, but as a personal designation. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 9:35. The available lexical meaning gives the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role in the passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Nōadia” or “Noathia.” It identifies a person by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The supplied references show that the same name is used across genealogical and post-exilic records, but the surrounding verse text is needed to identify which individual is meant in each occurrence.

This adjective means “painful,” describing something that causes or involves pain. It can refer to an experience marked by distress or suffering rather than something pleasant or harmless. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in passages from 1 Kings, Jeremiah, and Lamentations. The surrounding verse determines whether the pain is physical, emotional, or connected with a grievous situation, but the word itself centers on the quality of being painful.

This Greek LXX verb means “have compassion”: to feel and express mercy toward someone in need or distress. It describes a compassionate response rather than merely noticing another person’s situation. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly for compassion directed toward people. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “name” and can also describe something “notable.” As a noun, it identifies a person, place, or thing by its name and can point to the recognized identity or reputation associated with that name. It is broadly used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 947 times in this LXX corpus. Its normal sense remains a designation or recognized name, while the surrounding passage determines what person, place, or thing is being named.

This word means “not yet”. It is an adverb that says something has not happened or is not true up to the stated time, while leaving open the possibility that it may happen later. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it appears seven times, including passages from Genesis, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its meaning is straightforward, but the surrounding sentence determines what event or condition is being delayed or denied.

This adjective describes something directed toward the sky or belonging to heaven—something “skyward” or “heavenly.” It can characterize a direction, quality, or reality associated with heaven rather than earthly things. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs six times, all in 2, 3, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the noun or idea it describes, but its central sense remains connected with the sky or heaven.

This noun means a belt, an item worn around the waist. It names a tangible piece of clothing rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 18:11. The word’s basic meaning remains simple and concrete; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This verb means to stoop near or lean over. It describes bending forward toward something, often so that a person can look closely or draw near to what is below or in front of them. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, showing a recurring action rather than an abstract idea. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what the person bends toward and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “dispatch” or “send”—to cause someone or something to go toward a destination or appointed purpose. It can describe sending a person, messenger, or other thing, with the surrounding passage showing what is being sent and why. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, from Genesis through 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the act of sending rather than the destination itself.

Petephres, also rendered Petefris, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person connected with Joseph’s story. The name occurs five times, all in Genesis, from Genesis 37:36 through Genesis 46:20. Because names identify people rather than carry a broad vocabulary meaning, its significance here is its reference to this individual. The precise role of the person in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “foot” or “pace,” referring either to the body part used for walking or to a step and measured movement. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and can describe a person’s foot, the placing or washing of feet, or movement from one place to another. The word occurs 235 times in the Greek Old Testament, showing that it is a normal term for bodily movement and position. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun describes something “forestretching” or “jutting”—something that extends outward from what surrounds it. Its meaning is concrete and directional, drawing attention to a part that projects or sticks forward. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:6. The available information identifies its basic lexical sense but does not include the verse text, so the precise force of the word in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding passage.

This verb means “placed,” describing something put or set in a particular position. It presents placement as an action or condition rather than naming the object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times across 23 verses, especially in Leviticus and Numbers, where its meaning is understood from what has been put in place. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “put to use”: it describes using or making practical use of something. It is an action word, focusing on the act of employing something for a purpose rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the deliberate use of something available.

This Greek LXX noun means “Hrodioi; Rhodian,” identifying a person or people associated with Rhodes.
